newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major fights to move spotlight off Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major fights to move spotlight off Europe.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major fought on Thursday to dampen down speculation of a damaging cabinet rift over the government's policy on British entry into a single currency and to turn the spotlight off Europe.
But in a new blow, the former Conservative Foreign Secretary Lord Howe attacked Major's apparent hostility towards Europe and hinted he could consider withdrawing support for the government.
Former Conservative Prime Minister Edward Heath said the ruling party was without leadership and risked splitting up.

The new row over Europe erupted after Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, in what appeared to be a shift from a carefully hammered-out neutral cabinet policy agreed in January, said on Wednesday Britain was "on balance hostile" to EMU.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (Finance Minister) Kenneth Clarke immediately said his colleague must have made "a slip of the tongue", but Rifkind, fanning the flames of the acrimonious dispute, retorted that he had meant what he said.

In a late night effort to restore the cabinet's fragile equilibrium, the two met for a private drink at Rifkind's official central London residence, issuing a statement to Reuters that the government's position had not changed.

Stressing their hostility was due only to fears economic conditions for entry might be fudged for political reasons, they said: "We are (both) hostile to the notion that a single currency can proceed at any stage on a non-convergent basis."
But the statement failed to calm media speculation or the annoyance of pro-Europeans like Lord, formerly Geoffrey, Howe.

"The fact is that if it is perceived that we have a government that is in principle hostile to the concept of a single currency, then many people would feel reluctant to give continued support to that government," he told BBC radio.
Asked if that meant he would be reluctant to back Major, he added: "Of course, yes. One's enthusism is bound to diminish."

Heath, who secured Britain's entry into the European Community in 1973, also weighed in. "It is quite frightening because the prime minister is not giving leadership on this. It's because he wants to keep the peace in his party. Well, the leadership isn't there and the peace is lacking..."
"We don't want to break the (Conservative) party... (But) if we have more examples like the foreign secretary, we'll just have to break it... It could break after the election," he said.

Major fended off attempts to draw him into the row, telling parliament after he was quizzed by Labour leader Tony Blair there were arguments "in both directions" over the single currency and Britain was keeping its options open.

Aides from Major's Downing Street office also shrugged off Howe, now a member of the upper House of Lords and no threat to Major in the Commons, where the ruling party is tied at 322 seats with all the other parties combined.
"Lord Howe has to come to his own conclusions on the basis of government policy which has been spelled out with blinding clarity," one aide said.

But the continuing focus on the dispute overshadowed Major's attempts to switch the spotlight to the opposition Labour party's plans for devolution for Scotland and Wales, areas which the prime minister has targeted as key election issues.
Major must call a general election by May and his party trails Labour by around 20 points in polls.
Labour also turned the screw on Major.

Labour's economics spokesman Gordon Brown, in Washington for talks with U.S. Treasury Secretary Larry Rubin, set out five new tests that would have to be fulfilled before a Labour government would take the country into a single currency.

The five, which aides said made it less rather than more likely that Labour would take Britain into the currency if it starts as scheduled in 1999, include the impact on investment, jobs and financial services.
Brown said: "Getting it right is, of course, more important than getting it quickly."
